The punch biopsies show accumulation of finely granular basophilic material within follicular and sebaceous gland epithelium and Alcian blue–positive mucin, with a moderate perivascular/periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate and no cytologic atypia, epidermotropism, or basal vacuolar change. These histologic features are characteristic of follicular mucinosis (also called alopecia mucinosa) — mucin within follicular epithelium/sebaceous glands is the defining finding. In children this is most often an idiopathic (primary) localized process and the absence of atypical lymphocytes or systemic findings argues against an associated cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma. Other considerations include folliculotropic mycosis fungoides (can produce follicular mucinosis but usually shows atypical lymphocytes and occurs in older patients), common follicular disorders (keratosis pilaris, bacterial folliculitis, acneiform eruptions) which fit the clinical follicular papular morphology but do not explain the mucin histology, and disorders of dermal mucin deposition (papular mucinosis/lichen myxedematosus) which show dermal mucin rather than follicular mucin.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Primary (idiopathic) follicular mucinosis (alopecia mucinosa), localized/juvenile form — most likely given follicular mucin on Alcian blue, lymphocytic infiltrate without atypia, young age, facial distribution, and benign course.
2. Folliculotropic mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma with follicular mucinosis) — important differential because it can produce similar histologic changes, but less likely here because of the patient’s very young age and lack of cytologic atypia or systemic signs.
3. Keratosis pilaris / lichen spinulosus (follicular keratotic papular disorder) — clinically can present with multiple follicular papules in children; less likely because histology would show follicular hyperkeratosis rather than mucin deposition.
4. Bacterial or inflammatory folliculitis / acneiform eruption — may produce follicular papules on the face but typically shows neutrophilic infiltrate or follicular destruction and no Alcian blue–positive mucin.
5. Papular mucinosis (lichen myxedematosus) or other dermal mucinoses — can present with papules and mucin deposition, but these classically have dermal mucin and fibroblast proliferation rather than predominant mucin within follicular and sebaceous epithelium as seen here.
